entries.modern_form: PIE *meit(h)- / *meyt- 'to dwell, stay; staying place' (Pokorny 715 meit(h)-1 'staying (place)'; Walde-Pokorny II 247)
entries.note: Pokorny's lemma on the very page Nourai cites is 'meit(h)-1, Meaning: staying (place)', and its whole Iranian material is exactly what Nourai puts in the Avestan box (maēθanam 'dwelling, house', miθnaiti 'stays, dwells'). The language label 'Indo-European' and the gloss 'to stay' are therefore both right, and the double citation form 'Meit, Meith' reproduces Pokorny's own bracketed '(h)'. Two caveats that do not affect the verdict: (a) Pokorny prints a second, homophonous lemma meit(h)-2 'to exchange, change' on the same p.715, and modern handbooks (Wiktionary's *meytH-, Edelman EDIV V s.v. *(1)mait-) increasingly treat the 'dwell' and 'exchange' groups as one root, so Wiktionary reaches Persian mehmān through *meytH- 'to change, exchange'; (b) outside Iranian and Baltic the root has almost no material, so it is a small, well-attested but narrowly based reconstruction. Downstream, the Persian box is fully sound; the only soft spot on this chart is that Avestan maēθman- is a reconstruction, not an attested word (see node #1).

nodes.derivation: Two of the three forms are solidly Avestan, the third is a reconstruction. (1) 'maĕt' = the root maēθ- 'to dwell, stay', whose attested present is miθnaiti 'he dwells, stays' (nasal present *mit-na-, zero grade of maēθ-); Pokorny 715 quotes exactly this form. (2) 'maĕthanam' = Av. maēθana- n. 'dwelling, abode, station', cited in the accusative/nominative singular maēθanəm/maēθanam, which is how it appears throughout Yasna, the Yašts and the Vendīdād; Pokorny glosses it 'residence for people and gods, dwelling, house', and the Pahlavi Zand renders it māyān/mān 'house, home'. Nourai's gloss 'staying place, house, homeland' adds the later Persian 'homeland' sense, which belongs to New Persian mihan rather than to the Avestan word. (3) 'maĕthman' 'guest' is NOT attested in the extant Avesta: Hübschmann (Persische Studien pp.141–142) reconstructs it with an asterisk, 'mihmān "Gast" aus mehmān ... zd. *maiθman-', and in his sound-law list writes 'Ap. θm = np. hm: mihmān "Gast" = ap. *maiθman-'. Nourai prints it without an asterisk, as though attested; the derivation itself (a -man- stem from maēθ-, literally 'one who stays') is the standard one and is repeated by Mo'in. Hence 'plausible': the arrow root→Avestan is right, but one of the three Avestan words is a starred form.

nodes.derivation: Both words show the Iranian cluster θ + nasal turning into h + nasal in Middle Persian, the sound law Hübschmann formulated as 'Old Iranian θm = New Persian hm'. (1) Old Iranian *maiθman- 'one who stays, lodger' > MP mēhmān, written m(ʾ)hmʾn', glossed by MacKenzie 'inhabitant, guest; acceptable' > NP mehmān مهمان; the by-form mihmān/mīhmān میهمان arises by the ordinary raising of pretonic ē > i before the following long syllable (Hübschmann: 'mihmān aus mehmān'), and the spelling with yāʾ is the one Ferdowsi-era and later poets use, as in the couplet Nourai quotes. Cognates confirm the shape: Pashto melma 'guest' (pl. melmā), Sarikoli mehmūn, Baluchi, Kurdish mêwan/mîwan, Awromani mēhmān. (2) Old Iranian maēθana- 'dwelling' > MP mēhan (MacKenzie 'home') > NP mihan میهن 'home, homeland, birthplace'; the same θn > hn is fossilised in the Khorasani place-names Mihana, Kešmihan (< *kaš-maēθana-) and Xarmihan. Mo'in adds that the Pahlavi Zand of Vendīdād 8 renders Avestan maēθana- by mān ud xānag, and that the Avesta manuscript variants actually write 'mihan ud xānag'. The semantic step 'dwelling' → 'homeland' is Persian and post-Islamic; the older dictionaries (Sorūri, Borhān, Anjoman-ārā) still gloss mihan only 'house and home, resting place, birthplace'.
nodes.derivation_fa: «مهمان» و «میهن» هر دو نمونهٔ همان دگرگونیِ آوایی‌اند که هوبشمان فرمول‌بندی کرده است: خوشهٔ ایرانیِ باستانِ θ + خیشومی در فارسی میانه به h + خیشومی بدل می‌شود. ایرانیِ باستان *maiθman- «آن‌که می‌ماند، فرودآمده» به فارسی میانهٔ mēhmān (املای مانوی/پهلوی m’hmʾn) رسیده — مکنزی آن را «ساکن، مهمان» معنی کرده — و از آن «مهمان» فارسی نو؛ صورتِ «میهمان» با تحول ē به i در هجای پیش از تکیه پدید آمده («مهمان > میهمان»، هوبشمان). هم‌ریشه‌ها این ساخت را تأیید می‌کنند: پشتوی melma، سریکلیِ mehmūn، کردیِ mêwan/mîwan، اورامانیِ mēhmān. اوستاییِ maēθana- «خانه، جایگاه» نیز به پهلویِ mēhan و از آن به «میهن» رسیده است؛ همین θn > hn در نام‌جای‌های خراسان مانند «میهنه»، «کشمیهن» و «خرمیهن» به‌جا مانده. معین در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع (ص ۲۰۸۴) می‌افزاید که در زندِ فرگرد هشتمِ وندیداد maēθana- به «مان و خانگ» ترجمه شده و در نسخه‌بدل‌های اوستا «میهن و خانک» نوشته‌اند. تحول معناییِ «خانه» به «وطن» فارسی و پس از اسلام است؛ فرهنگ‌های کهن (سروری، برهان، انجمن‌آرا) «میهن» را تنها «خان و مان، آرامگاه، زادبوم» معنی کرده‌اند. ادعای نورایی درست است.

entries.modern_form: PIE *mel- / *melh₂- 'dark, dirty; of a darkish colour' (Pokorny mel-6, melə- 720–721; Watkins/AHD mel-2 'of a darkish color')
entries.note: Pokorny's lemma 'mel-6, melə-: dark colour (black, dirty, etc.)' runs over pp.720–721, i.e. it begins on the page Nourai cites, and Watkins prints 'mel-2. Of a darkish color. 1. Greek melas, black: MELANO-; MELANCHOLY, PSILOMELANE. [Pok. 6. mel- 720.]' — same page number, same gloss. The material (Skt. malina- 'dirty', Gk. μέλας 'black', Latvian melns 'black', Lith. mélas 'blue', OPrus. melne 'blue stain', Lith. mólis 'loam, clay') fully justifies the double gloss 'black, dirty'. Interesting for the next entry: Pokorny's own note on this lemma says 'Root/lemma: melo-, smelo-: small animal, derived from Root/lemma: mel-6, melə-: dark colour', i.e. Pokorny attaches Nourai's Mel 2 'Melo/Smelo' branch to THIS root rather than to *mel- 'to deceive'. The chart's chain is right down to the Greek; the two Latin/Persian links below it are where it goes wrong (nodes #2 and #3).
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ هندواروپاییِ آغازینِ *mel- «سیاه، تیره، چرکین» است. پوکورنی مدخل «mel-6, melə-: رنگ تیره (سیاه، چرکین و مانند آن)» را در صفحات ۷۲۰–۷۲۱ آورده — یعنی درست همان صفحه‌ای که نورایی ارجاع می‌دهد — و واتکینز در پیوستِ ریشه‌های هندواروپاییِ فرهنگ آمریکن هریتیج می‌نویسد «mel-2: از رنگی تیره؛ یونانی melas «سیاه»؛ MELANCHOLY» و همان شمارهٔ صفحهٔ ۷۲۰ را می‌دهد. گواه‌ها (سنسکریت malina- «چرکین»، یونانی μέλας «سیاه»، لتونی melns، لیتوانی mólis «گِل») هر دو معنای «سیاه» و «چرکین» را تأیید می‌کند؛ پس ادعای نورایی درست است. نکتهٔ باریک آنکه پوکورنی خودِ شاخهٔ melo-/smelo- (که نورایی زیر «Mel 2» گذاشته) را برخاسته از همین ریشهٔ mel-6 می‌داند.

nodes.derivation: The two elements are exactly right, the compound as printed is Nourai's own analytic form. μέλας, gen. μέλανος 'black' continues *mel-n-, the n-stem of PIE *mel- 'dark' (Pokorny 720); χολή 'bile, gall' belongs to PIE *ǵʰel-/*ghel- 'to shine; yellow, green' — precisely Nourai's cross-reference ☞Ghel, and precisely Watkins's double etymology 'MELANCHOLY ghel-2, mel-2'. The compound actually attested in Greek, however, is not *μελαγχολή but μελαγχολία (Hippocratic corpus, 5th–4th c. BCE, in the humoral theory of the four fluids), beside the adjective μελάγχολος and the verb μελαγχολάω; the neuter μέλαινα χολή 'black bile' is the underlying phrase. So 'melan-xolĕ' should be read as Nourai's hyphenated analysis 'melan- + kholē', not as a citable Greek lemma; the gloss 'black bile, mental disorder' correctly gives both the literal and the medical sense, the second having arisen because an excess of the black humour was held to cause despondency and madness.
nodes.derivation_fa: دو جزءِ این ترکیب کاملاً درست است، امّا صورتی که نورایی چاپ کرده تجزیهٔ خودِ اوست نه واژه‌ای گواه‌دار. μέλας (حالت اضافی μέλανος) «سیاه» از *mel-n- است، یعنی ستاکِ نون‌دارِ همان ریشهٔ هندواروپاییِ *mel- «تیره» (پوکورنی ۷۲۰)؛ و χολή «زَهره، صفرا» به ریشهٔ *ǵʰel- «درخشیدن، زرد و سبز» می‌رسد — همان ارجاعِ «☞Ghel» که نورایی داده و همان دو ریشه‌ای که واتکینز برای melancholy برمی‌شمارد. ولی ترکیبی که در یونانی گواه دارد μελαγχολία است (در پیکرهٔ بقراطی، سدهٔ پنجم و چهارم پیش از میلاد، در نظریهٔ چهار خلط)، در کنارِ صفتِ μελάγχολος؛ عبارتِ بنیادین هم μέλαινα χολή «صفرای سیاه» است. پس «melan-xolĕ» را باید تجزیهٔ ساختواژی خواند، نه سرواژهٔ یونانی. معنایی که نورایی داده («صفرای سیاه، اختلال روانی») درست است: معنای پزشکی از این باور برخاسته که فزونیِ خلطِ سوداوی سبب افسردگی و دیوانگی می‌شود. ادعای نورایی با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: There is no Latin word 'melancholy'. The Latin form is melancholia, a straight transliteration of Greek μελαγχολία taken over by the Latin medical writers (Late Latin, in Caelius Aurelianus and the translations of the Greek physicians) and kept in the medieval scholastic vocabulary of the four humours; 'melancholy' is the English (and, as melancolie, the Old French) shape of the word, three steps further down the chain. I rendered PDF page 329 at 200 dpi and read the printed box: the book itself prints 'melancholy' in the Latin node, so the extraction is faithful and the error is Nourai's own — he has filled the Latin slot with the English descendant. The chain the box is meant to carry is Greek μελαγχολία → Late Latin melancholia → Old French melancolie (13th c.) → Middle English melancolie (c.1300); a second consequence of the misprint is that the arrow Latin→English on this chart short-circuits the Old French stage that every dictionary records.

nodes.derivation: The word is genuine and its ultimate source is genuinely Greek μελαγχολία, but the parent drawn on the chart is wrong: Persian مالیخولیا did not come from Latin. It is an Arabic-mediated Graeco-Arabic medical term. Greek μελαγχολία was rendered in Syriac and then in the 9th-century Arabic translations of Galen and the Hippocratic writings made in the circle of Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq (d. 873) as مالنخوليا mālinḫūliyā, with the by-forms ماليخوليا mālīḫūliyā (n > y before the ḫ, an Arabic scribal/dissimilatory shift) and the clipped ماخوليا māḫūliyā; from the Arabic medical literature it passed into Persian, where the Arabic loan-shape with mā- for Greek me- and the -iyā ending betray the route. Wiktionary states the Persian word is a 'misspelling of earlier مالنخولیا (mâlenxuliyâ), from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία', with the variant ماخولیا 'through Arabic'; Dehkhoda labels the entry «معرب» (arabicised) and Moʿin «مأخوذ از یونانی» (taken from Greek). Latin plays no part: there is no Latin phase in the transmission of Greek medicine into Persian, which went Greek → Syriac → Arabic → Persian. The chart's semantic gloss 'melancholy' is right; the Persian sense is 'a cerebral disorder producing delusions and fantasies', i.e. still the humoral disease name, and the Borhān glosses it «کوفت و خلل دماغی و سودا و خیال خام».

nodes.derivation: The English word is a real descendant of the Greek compound, but one stage is missing from the chart. Late Latin melancholia gave Old French melancolie 'black bile; ill disposition, anger, annoyance' (13th c.), with the popular variant malencolie produced by association with mal 'sickness, ill'; Middle English took over both shapes about 1300 as melancolie / malencolie in the sense 'mental disorder marked by sullenness, gloom, irritability', and the weakened sense 'sorrow, gloom' is in place by the mid-14th century. The learned respelling with -ch- (after Latin melancholia) and the ending -y for -ie give the modern melancholy. When the humoral physiology behind the word lost credit in the 18th century the word kept only its psychological meaning. So the arrow Latin→English is right in substance but skips Old French, which is where the mal- variant and the whole medieval semantic range come from.

entries.modern_form: two Pokorny lemmas: *mel-2 'to fail; to deceive' (Pokorny 719–720; Watkins mel-7) and *melo-, *smelo- 'small animal' (Pokorny 724; Watkins mel-5 'bad')
entries.note: Every piece of Nourai's root box is in the sources, but the box itself is his own synthesis of two entries that Pokorny and Watkins keep apart. (1) Pokorny 719–720 'mel-2, Meaning: to fail; to deceive' has precisely the Avestan word of node #1: 'Avestan mairya- "deceitful, knavish, villainous"; Armenian mel "sin"; Gk. μέλεος "futile, worthless, wretched"; MIr. mell "fault, error", mairle "evil, harm"; Lith. mēlas "lie"'. (2) Pokorny 724 'melo-, smelo-, Meaning: small animal' has precisely nodes #3 and #8: 'Gr. μῆλον "small cattle, sheep"; OIr. mil "(small) animal" ... There "small cattle" could be an old nominalization of an Adj. meaning "small" ... Old Bulgarian malŭ "small", Latin malus "evil, bad" (as "small"), Oscan mallom "malum" ... with anl. s-: Gothic smals, OHG/OS smal, OE smæl "small, little, narrow", Old Icelandic smali n. "small animal"'. Nourai's citation POK:719,724 therefore names both lemmas honestly, and his composite gloss 'small, insignificant, also bad and harmful' is a fair summary of the two. What is his own is the claim that they are one root: Pokorny does not say so — he derives melo-/smelo- from mel-6 'dark colour' (= Nourai's Mel 1!), and keeps mel-2 'deceive' separate; Watkins likewise splits them into mel-5 'Bad' [Pok. mēlo- 724] and mel-7 'To miss, deceive' [Pok. 2. mel- 719]. Buck (16.72 BAD, p.1177 — the page Nourai cites on node #1) leaves the choice open: 'Lat. malus ... etym. dub., perh. fr. the root in Ir. mellaim "deceive" ... Av. mairya- "deceitful", etc.; or : OE smel, OHG smal, etc. "small"?' — that is, Buck presents exactly Nourai's two halves as rival explanations of one word, which is the closest anyone comes to endorsing the merger. Nourai's own hedge in the root box ('These words may be related to root "Mer 2: harm, die"') is well judged and is where modern Iranology stands for the mairya-/mār branch (see node #1).

nodes.derivation: The word and the gloss are exactly right, the parentage is genuinely contested — and Nourai's own NOTE says so, which is to his credit. Avestan mairiia-/mairya- is a well-attested adjective of the Younger Avesta: Bartholomae, Altiranisches Wörterbuch col. 1151, 'mairya- Adj. (fem. -ya-) "betrügerisch, tückisch, schurkisch; Schurke"' — 'deceitful, treacherous, villainous; villain' — used of Frangrasyan, of the karapans, of demons and of witches (Yt.5.18, 22; Y.9.18; V.5.35), and Horn (Grundriss p.283, no.129) records the Pahlavi continuation 'mar "verderblich, schädlich"' with the same gloss Nourai gives, 'harmful, evil'. Formally mairya- is *mar-ya- with the regular Avestan epenthesis a > ai before -y-. On the parent there are two camps. (a) Pokorny 719 and Walde–Pokorny II 291 put mairya- under *mel-2 'to fail, deceive' (with MIr. mell 'fault', Lith. mēlas 'lie'), which requires *mel-yo- > Iranian *mar-ya- by the ordinary Indo-Iranian l > r; and Buck p.1177 lists this among the possible sources of Latin malus. This is Nourai's source and it is a respectable position. (b) Bartholomae's own arrangement, Horn's cross-reference to his no.977 (merg 'death', √mar 'to die'), Moʿin's footnote in the Borhān (p.1934), Nyberg and the Shāyest nē Shāyest glossary all connect mairya- with the root mar- 'to die', causative 'to kill' (Skt. māra- 'killer, destroyer'), i.e. PIE *mer-. That is now the majority Iranological view, and it is exactly what Nourai's NOTE reports. Verdict 'plausible': the word, language and gloss are confirmed; the arrow from *mel- is one of two live options and probably the minority one.

nodes.derivation: The Persian word is certain and its family is certain; what is uncertain is the exact Iranian preform, and with it whether the arrow should come from mairya- or from a sister formation. New Persian مار mār 'snake' continues Middle Persian mār, written m'l, glossed 'snake' by MacKenzie and attested in the Pahlavi Dēnkard/Wizīdagīhā passages that Nyberg lists (¹mār [m'l] 'snake', 76.9, 86.15, 96.25, 98.12–15; Nyberg also has the Zand gloss mār-bānak for the snake-like karpōk). Moʿin's footnote in the Borhān (p.1934, fn.4) gives precisely Nourai's chain and its root: «پهلوی mār. قس سانسکریت māra ... این کلمهٔ سانسکریت بمعنی میراننده و کشنده است. بنابراین با کلمهٔ اوستایی mairya بمعنی زیانکار و تباه‌کننده یکی است، از مصدر mar اوستایی و پارسی باستان بمعنی مردن» — 'Pahlavi mār; cf. Sanskrit māra "killer"; therefore identical with Avestan mairya "harmful, destroying", from the Avestan and Old Persian verb mar- "to die"'. Horn (p.283 no.129 → p.219 no.977) says the same in German, adding that the Ossetic parallel marg 'poison' beside 'death' justifies deriving 'snake' from √mar 'die' / caus. 'kill': the snake is 'the killer', a euphemism of the same kind as Persian کرم 'worm/dragon'. The one wrinkle is the vowel: MP mār has ā where mairya- has short a plus -y-, so Wiktionary and most handbooks posit Old Iranian *māra- (a lengthened-grade agent noun, Skt. māra- 'killer') rather than a direct continuation of mairya-. mairya- and mār are thus cousins from the same verbal root rather than parent and child. Hence 'plausible': the arrow is the one Nourai's own references draw, but the strictly correct preform is *māra-, and the ultimate root is *mer- 'to die', not *mel-.

nodes.derivation: The first pair is Latin and correctly derived; the second item is not Latin. (1) Latin malus 'bad, evil' and the adverb male 'badly, ill' (whence malignus 'ill-natured, harmful' = male + -gnus, and malitia > malice) are exactly what Watkins puts under 'mel-5. Bad. Latin malus, bad, and male, ill (> malignus, harmful) ... [Pok. mēlo- 724]', and Pokorny 724 spells out the semantics: Latin malus 'evil, bad' is the same word as OCS malŭ 'small' and Oscan mallom, i.e. 'bad' from 'small, of inferior value' — precisely Nourai's root gloss. Klein makes the same connection s.v. small: 'prob. also with L. malus, "bad" (prop. "insignificant, of inferior value")'. Ernout–Meillet and Walde–Hofmann, quoted by Buck, call the etymology 'dub.'. (2) 'mal-aria' is Italian, not Latin: it is mal'aria, a contraction of Italian mala aria 'bad air' (mala fem. of malo < malus, aria < Latin āēr < Greek ἀήρ, whence Nourai's cross-reference ☞Wē 1 to the 'blow' root). No such compound exists in Latin; classical Latin would say malus āēr. Putting it in the Latin box is an anachronism of a stage — its proper home is the Italian node directly below, which Nourai leaves empty. The gloss 'bad (sick) air' is right, and reflects the pre-germ-theory belief that the fevers of marshland were caused by its exhalations.

nodes.derivation: A pass-through node with no word printed on the page; the word it stands for is Italian mal'aria (also written mala aria, malaria) 'bad air'. Italian malo/mala continues Latin malus/mala with the normal loss of final -us and the Tuscan outcome of the a-stem feminine, and aria continues Latin āēr (accusative āera) 'air' through the Vulgar Latin *āria; the elision in mal'aria is the ordinary Italian apocope before a vowel. The compound is a term of 17th–18th-century Italian medicine for the noxious exhalation of the Campagna and the Pontine marshes; Klein records that it 'was prob. used first by the Italian physician Francisco Torti (1658–1741)'. It is from this Italian phrase, not from anything Latin, that all the European forms of the word descend, so the node is where the chain really begins.

nodes.derivation: Persian مالاریا mālāriyā is a straightforward modern European loanword, borrowed as a whole with no Persian morphology: Italian mal'aria → French malaria → Persian مالاریا, entering Persian with the Western medicine of the late Qajar and early Pahlavi period (it is absent from the classical dictionaries and from the Borhān, and appears in Moʿin's volume of foreign compounds, which is the reference Nourai cites). The Persian spelling shows the loan character plainly: the word is written with alef for both long ā's and yā for the -i-, it is not analysable in Persian, and it coexists with the native descriptive term تب نوبه tab-e nawba 'intermittent fever', which is how Moʿin actually defines it ('تب نوبه، بیماری گرمسیری که بر اثر گزش پشهٔ آنوفل در بدن انسان پدید می‌آید'). Nothing in the chain from PIE *melo- 'small' through Latin malus to this word is in doubt except the intermediate node labels discussed above (the compound is Italian, not Latin).

nodes.derivation: Five of the six are correct Latin-based derivatives, the sixth is the Italian word again. malicious < Old French malicious < Latin malitiōsus, from malitia 'badness' (malus + -itia); malady < Middle English maladie < Old French maladie, from malade 'sick' < Late Latin male habitus 'ill-kept, in bad condition' (Klein s.v. malady); malignant < Latin malignāns, present participle of malignāre, from malignus 'ill-natured' = male + the root of gignere/-gnus 'born, natured'; dismal < Anglo-French dis mal < Medieval Latin diēs malī 'evil days', the two unlucky days of each month in the medieval calendar, whence the modern sense 'gloomy'; malfunction is a 20th-century English formation on the learned prefix mal- (< Old French mal < Latin male). All five appear in Watkins's own list under mel-5: 'MAL-, MALICE, MALIGN; DISMAL, MALADY, MALEDICT, MALEFACTOR, MALEVOLENT, MALVERSATION'. malaria, however, is not from Latin: English took it from Italian mal'aria in 1740 (first in Horace Walpole's letters), and Watkins pointedly does NOT list MALARIA under mel-5. So the node's contents are right but heterogeneous, and the Latin→English arrow is a compression: every one of these words except malfunction reached English through French, not directly from Latin.

nodes.derivation: The form and the family are right; the gloss belongs to a different member of the family. Proto-Germanic *smalaz is an ADJECTIVE 'small, narrow, slender' — Gothic smals (superlative smalista 'smallest'), Old Saxon and Old High German smal, MHG smal, German schmal 'narrow', Middle Dutch/Dutch smal, Old English smæl 'narrow, slim, slender, fine, small'. The meaning 'small animal, small cattle' belongs to the substantivised neuter Old Norse smali 'small cattle, sheep' and to the Old High German compounds smala-nōz, smalaz fihu, MHG smal-nōz, smal-vihe 'young/small livestock' and smal-hirte 'herdsman of small cattle' — all of which Pokorny 724 lists immediately after the adjective. So 'smal : small animal' conflates the adjective with its nominal derivative; the underlying etymology, however, is exactly Nourai's, and Pokorny's own comment makes the animal sense secondary: '"small cattle" could be an old nominalization of an Adj. meaning "small"'. The s- is the mobile s- (Pokorny writes *smə-lo- beside *melo-), which is why the root box gives both Melo and Smelo; outside Germanic the s-less form appears in Greek μῆλον 'small cattle, sheep', Armenian mal 'sheep, ram' and Old Irish mil '(small) animal'.

nodes.derivation: Old English smæl 'narrow, slender, fine; small, quiet' > Middle English smal, smale (plural/inflected), also smel > Modern English small; the doubling of the -ll- is an English orthographic convention (as in all, tall) and the vowel is the regular reflex of OE æ before a single consonant. Old English smæl continues Proto-West Germanic *smal, Proto-Germanic *smalaz, from PIE *(s)mel-o- 'small' — Wiktionary's chain exactly. The semantic history runs the other way from Germanic's sisters: English generalised the adjective to the ordinary word for 'little' and lost the 'narrow' sense that German schmal kept, while the 'small cattle' noun survives only in dialect and in the fossilised smallholder. Klein's entry (p.1461) covers the whole chain, and Watkins's index gives 'SMALL mēlo-'.
